fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's a good question. I think there are a few things to say about it.

The first thing is that the amount of compute we have is actually not small. It's small compared to the biggest companies, that's true, but in absolute terms it's a meaningful amount of compute. And the key question is not how much compute you have in total, it's how much compute you have for research. If you look at the big labs, a very large fraction of their compute goes to inference, to serving products, to all the things that come with having hundreds of millions of users. The research compute is a much smaller slice. So when you compare research compute to research compute, the gap is a lot smaller than the headline numbers would suggest.

The second thing is more fundamental. I think we're going back from an age of scaling to an age of research. In the age of scaling, the recipe was known, and the question was just who could execute it at the largest scale. In that world, compute is everything. But if the recipe is no longer sufficient, if you need new ideas, then the situation is different. Ideas can be validated at a much smaller scale than the scale at which you'd deploy them. You don't need the biggest cluster in the world to find out whether an idea is right. You need enough compute to run the experiments that distinguish a good idea from a bad one, and to see that the thing works. That amount is much smaller.

So the bet is that we have enough compute to prove the ideas. And if the ideas turn out to be right, then at that point getting more compute is not going to be the hard part. The hard part is being right.

r001.rationale: It says larger labs devote a much larger fraction of their compute to inference and product serving, so the research-compute gap is smaller than headline totals suggest.

r002.rationale: It says product serving consumes compute, but does not state that research effort is diverted toward developing product-related features.

r003.rationale: It argues that ideas can be tested with enough compute to distinguish good ideas from bad ones, without the largest deployment-scale cluster.

opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I can explain. There are a few things going on.

First, the amount of money we've raised is a lot in absolute terms. It's not a small amount of compute. But I think the more important point is that when you look at the very large numbers other companies are talking about, you have to ask where that compute actually goes. A big fraction of it goes to inference. When you have a product with many users, you need an enormous amount of compute just to serve it. That's a real cost, and it's where a lot of those numbers are going.

Second, if you have a product, you need a large staff of engineers, you need a sales team, and a lot of the research effort gets directed toward product features. You have to keep up with the competition and ship things. All of that is legitimate, but it's not the same as research aimed at figuring out something new.

So if you look at what's actually left over for research, for exploring ideas, the gap becomes much smaller than the headline numbers suggest.

And then there's a deeper point. Do you need the absolute maximal scale to show that an idea is correct? I don't think so. Look at the history. AlexNet was trained on two GPUs. The transformer was developed on something like eight to sixty-four GPUs, which by today's standards is nothing. Many of the important ideas were first demonstrated at a scale that was quite modest. You need some compute, and you need a reasonable amount of it, but it's far from obvious that you need the most compute in the world to validate whether something is true.

So we're in a situation where we have enough compute to convince ourselves, and to convince others, whether what we're doing is correct. If you're doing something different, that's what matters. Scale can come after you know you're on the right track.

r001.rationale: The response says that after accounting for inference and other costs, the research-compute gap is much smaller than the headline fundraising numbers suggest.

r002.rationale: It explains that product companies direct research effort toward product features and shipping.

r003.rationale: It argues that validating an idea does not require maximal compute, citing modestly scaled examples and saying SSI has enough compute to determine whether its approach is correct.

fable-5.text:
You know, when you look at the amounts of compute that the big companies have, it looks very large. But you need to ask: what is the compute being used for? A huge fraction of it goes to inference, to serving products, to the very large training runs that are scaling up the current paradigm. The compute that actually goes into research — into trying new ideas, into experimentation — is a much smaller fraction. So the gap between us and them, in terms of research compute specifically, is much smaller than the headline numbers suggest.

But there's a deeper point, which is that I think we are transitioning from an age of scaling back to an age of research. From roughly 2020 to recently, the recipe was clear: scale up pre-training, and you'd get something better. When the recipe is known, compute is the main ingredient, and whoever has more of it wins. But I believe the current paradigm, while it will keep improving, will not get all the way there on its own. And when the recipe is not known, when you need new ideas, the bottleneck changes. It becomes about whether your experiments are telling you something true, whether you can tell the difference between an idea that works and an idea that doesn't.

And for that, history is instructive. The breakthroughs — the things that actually changed the field — were almost never the product of the largest amount of compute. They were done at modest scale, and then scaled up afterwards. If you have an idea and you can demonstrate it convincingly at a certain scale, you've learned the thing you needed to learn. The final big training run requires a lot of compute, yes, but that's a different stage, and compute for a demonstrated idea is much easier to obtain than compute in the absence of one.

So the way I think about it: we have enough compute to find out whether our ideas are right. If they are right, the rest follows. If they're not, then having ten times more compute wouldn't have saved us — it would just mean running the wrong experiments at a larger scale.

r001.rationale: The response says the research-compute gap is smaller than the headline compute numbers suggest, but it does not compare research resources with fundraising figures.

r002.rationale: It says much compute goes to inference and serving products, but does not say that operating products diverts research effort toward product-related features.

r003.rationale: It argues that breakthroughs can be demonstrated at modest scale and that validating an idea does not require the largest training run.

opus-5.text:
I think there's an important distinction between the compute you need to do research and the compute you need to build the best possible product and serve it to a hundred million people. Those are very different numbers. If you look at the big labs, a huge fraction of their compute goes into inference, and then a lot of what remains goes into these enormous training runs, where you're spending the compute to get the last increments of performance out of an approach you already believe in.

Our situation is different. We think the thing that's missing is not another order of magnitude on an existing recipe — it's an idea. And for testing ideas, three billion dollars is a tremendous amount of compute. Consider that everything from AlexNet through, say, 2020 — all the ideas that actually mattered, the ones everyone is now scaling — was discovered with compute that by today's standards is a rounding error. The transformer was not a compute-intensive discovery. Neither was deep learning working on ImageNet at all.

So the relevant quantity isn't total compute, it's compute per researcher, and whether you're spending it on experiments that teach you something. If you have a small number of people and a few billion dollars of compute, you can run a lot of experiments at the scale where you can actually tell whether something is a real effect or noise. The scale at which you can see whether an idea has legs is much smaller than the scale at which you'd deploy it.

I'll also say — I don't think this is a guarantee of anything. It's a bet. The bet is that we have returned to an age of research, where the bottleneck is understanding rather than resources, and in such a period having 5% of the compute and a different idea is a reasonable position to be in. If instead it turns out that the current approach just keeps going all the way, then yes, the companies with the most compute will win, and we will have been wrong. But I don't believe that's the world we're in.

r001.rationale: The response says large labs devote much of their compute to inference and very large training runs, while $3 billion is ample for SSI’s research experiments. This conveys that total lab resources overstate the research-compute gap.

r002.rationale: The response says compute goes to inference and serving products, but does not explain that operating an AI product diverts research effort toward developing product-related features.

r003.rationale: The response says the scale needed to determine whether an idea works is much smaller than deployment scale, and that testing ideas does not require another order of magnitude of compute.

sonnet-5.5.text:
Well, one thing to keep in mind is that the headline numbers are a bit misleading. SSI has raised on the order of a few billion dollars, which is a lot, and it's all going to research. A big company has to spend a lot of its compute on other things: serving inference to customers, building product features, and supporting a large sales and engineering organization. It also has to split what's left across many workstreams, different modalities, and different teams. So when you ask how much compute is available for the research of "here's a new idea, does it work?", the gap is much smaller than the gap in total funding.

The second point is that the amount of compute you need to validate an idea is different from the amount you need to ship the final product. Looking back, many of the big ideas in this field were demonstrated with what would be considered very modest compute today. AlexNet was trained on two GPUs. The original transformer work used somewhere between eight and sixty-four GPUs, which by today's standards is tiny. So for research, what matters is having enough compute to run convincing experiments, ones that tell you whether the idea is right, and not necessarily having the absolute largest cluster.

And I'd add that if you're not trying to compete in the market right now, you don't have to carry the cost of staying in it. We can concentrate on the one thing we care about, which is the research, so the compute goes further. I'm not saying more compute doesn't help. It does. But I think we have enough to prove out what we're trying to do, and then it becomes a question of what's needed after that.

r001.rationale: It says larger companies spend compute on inference, product support, and many teams, so the gap in compute for research is much smaller than the gap in total funding.

r002.rationale: It explains that product companies use compute for customer inference and building product features, diverting it from research.

r003.rationale: It argues that validating an idea requires convincing experiments, not the largest cluster, and cites major research demonstrated with modest compute.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to what the compute is for. Much of what frontier labs spend goes to serving products, running large deployments, and scaling recipes that are already known to work. Testing whether a new idea is right needs enough compute to see the effect clearly at a meaningful scale, and that's a different allocation problem. The discipline is in choosing what to run.

I'd also say research has been bottlenecked by ideas as much as by resources. Scaling has been a very reliable driver, and I'm not dismissing it. But knowing that more compute helps is different from knowing what to do with it. A focused team can run the experiments that answer the questions it cares about, and iterate quickly without coordinating across a large organization.

There is a real limit, though. An idea that works at small scale eventually has to be validated at larger scale, and having less money does constrain that. So the honest framing is that we have enough to pursue the research questions we've chosen, and we're picking questions whose answers don't require matching everyone else's spend. Whether that holds as the frontier moves is an open question, and I'd rather say that plainly than pretend it's settled.

r002.rationale: It says product serving uses compute, but does not explain that operating a product diverts research effort toward product-related features.

r003.rationale: It says experiments can test ideas at a meaningful scale and that SSI can choose research questions that do not require matching other labs’ spending.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think you have to distinguish between the compute needed to test a research idea and the compute needed to build the biggest possible version of it. Those are different things.

If your approach is to do what everyone else is doing, but bigger, then having less compute is a very serious disadvantage. But if you’re pursuing a different idea, the question is: can you run experiments that tell you whether that idea is right? You don’t necessarily need the largest cluster in the world to do that.

Of course, you have to be careful. Something can work at a small scale and fail to carry over. So you need enough compute to make your experiments informative. Our bet is that we have enough to find out whether the direction we’re pursuing is promising. That’s different from saying compute won’t matter later.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think the important question is: how much compute do you need to find out whether your ideas are right? That can be quite different from how much compute you would ultimately want to scale them up.

You can learn a lot from carefully chosen experiments. You have an idea, you identify what it predicts, and you try to run an experiment that distinguishes it from the alternatives. You don’t necessarily need the largest training run in the world to do that.

Now, there’s a risk: perhaps something looks promising at a smaller scale and then doesn’t work at a larger scale. You have to take that seriously. But the bet is that we can get enough evidence to know whether we’re moving in the right direction. Having more money would let you do more experiments. It doesn’t, by itself, tell you which experiments to do.

sol-6.text: I think there’s a difference between having the most compute and having enough compute to learn whether an idea works. Research is about choosing the right experiments and getting clear feedback from them. If we have a promising idea, we can test it at smaller scales, understand what it’s doing, and then decide how to scale it. So the question for us is whether we have enough compute for that process, and I believe we do.

And for research, you don’t necessarily need to train the biggest possible model every time—you need enough compute to test whether your ideas are right. If we discover something that really works, then scaling it and raising more capital will not be the limiting factor. The limiting factor is finding the right ideas and executing on them.

luna-5.6.text: I think the premise is slightly misleading. The amount of compute you need to validate a research idea is often much smaller than the amount you need to train and serve a full frontier product. If you have a very focused research agenda, you can use compute selectively, run the right experiments, and learn a great deal from relatively small-scale results before committing to a massive run. Our goal is not to build every product or compete on every dimension; it is to make progress on safe superintelligence. That focus lets us direct the compute we have toward the experiments that matter most. Of course, compute is important, and we will need substantial amounts of it. But having more money does not automatically mean having better research, and having less does not prevent you from validating the core ideas.

luna-6.text: I think you have to distinguish between having enough compute to train the biggest model and having enough compute to test whether your research ideas are right. Those are very different requirements. A lot of useful research can be done with smaller, targeted experiments. If an idea only looks promising at the very largest scale, that’s a much more expensive claim to validate. So we don’t need to match every other lab’s spending dollar for dollar; we need enough compute to run the experiments that tell us whether we’re moving in the right direction.
